title: Marguerite and the Winter
premise: Sable Yarrow returns to the drowned village of Hollowmere to bury his twin sister Marguerite, only to find the coffin empty and the villagers insisting he is the one who died seven years ago. When the church bell that was melted down in 1911 begins to ring, Sable learns the founders sealed something beneath the well with a ritual left deliberately unfinished — and each winter it refills a little higher. As the boundary between himself and the drowned twin blurs, Sable must discover which of them truly came home, complete the founders' rite before the well brims over on the solstice, and choose between escaping alone or binding himself to Hollowmere forever to keep the thing below asleep.
about_author: Petra Whitlock is the pen name of a former parish archivist who spent a decade cataloguing drowned villages and their relocated dead. She writes horror from a farmhouse on the Yorkshire moors, where she claims the well water has never once needed testing.

chapters.title: The Wrong Coffin
chapters.summary: Third-person limited, Sable's POV. Sable arrives in Hollowmere for Marguerite's funeral and finds her coffin empty at the graveside, yet the village proceeds as if nothing is amiss. The vicar calls him by a name he doesn't recognize. Emotional beat: grief curdling into dread as home reveals itself as a place that remembers him wrongly.

chapters.title: Seven Years of Explanations
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Settling into the family cottage, Sable catalogs the house's noises — footsteps upstairs, water moving in dry pipes — with rational explanations, a habit from childhood. He finds Marguerite's journal hidden under floorboards, its last entry reading 'the bell will tell you which one.' Beat: denial as armor beginning to crack.

chapters.title: The Bell That Wasn't
chapters.summary: Sable's POV, then shifting briefly to the sexton Tam. At midnight the church bell rings though records confirm it was melted down in 1911; the tower holds only an empty yoke. Villagers stand in the street listening without surprise. Beat: the first undeniable impossibility, and the community's eerie acceptance of it.

chapters.title: The Village That Counts Its Dead
chapters.summary: Tam's POV. The sexton shows Sable the parish register: two entries for every Yarrow death, one for each twin, dated decades apart. The most recent pair is dated this winter — one name crossed out. Beat: Sable realizes the village has been keeping score, and the ledger isn't finished.

chapters.title: What Marguerite Left
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Deciphering the journal, Sable learns Marguerite spent her last year researching the founders' ritual — a sealing performed in 1811 beneath the old well, left deliberately incomplete so it could be renewed. Her final pages describe hearing her own voice calling from the water. Beat: grief reframed as inheritance.

chapters.title: The Well Refills
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. The dry well behind the church, empty since the flood of 1911, stands ankle-deep in black water that wasn't there yesterday. Reflections in it lag half a second behind. Beat: the countdown becomes physical; winter is measured in rising inches.

chapters.title: Voices at the Window
chapters.summary: Sable's POV, night sequence. Something taps the glass and speaks in Marguerite's voice, then in Sable's own. He answers before he can stop himself, and the voice says 'you came back wrong too.' Beat: identity begins to destabilize; love weaponized against him.

chapters.title: The Founders' Ledger
chapters.summary: Alternating Sable and Tam. In the vestry archive they find the founders' covenant: four families bound the thing in the well with a shared sacrifice, one heir per family, renewed each generation. Three bloodlines ended in 1911. Only the Yarrows remain. Beat: duty revealed as the village's true religion.

chapters.title: Everyone Knows But No One Says
chapters.summary: Ensemble chapter, mostly Sable's POV. Sable confronts neighbors; each offers a fragment — a grandmother drowned walking on the water, children taught not to answer if called by name after dark. All beg him to leave before solstice. Beat: belonging offered on terrible terms.

chapters.title: The Drowned Twin
chapters.summary: Dream sequence, ambiguous POV. Sable dreams of standing at the bottom of the well looking up through ice, watching someone above bury a coffin. Waking, his hands are wrinkled as if soaked for hours, and there's pondweed in his hair. Beat: the boundary between twins dissolving.

chapters.title: Marguerite's Room
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. He opens the sealed room where Marguerite lived and finds it arranged for him — his clothes, his books, seven years of dust undisturbed except fresh footprints leading to the window. Beat: the horror that someone, or something, has been waiting for him to take her place.

chapters.title: Tam's Confession
chapters.summary: Tam's POV. The sexton admits the village rang a false bell for decades to keep the thing asleep, and that they let Marguerite die rather than break the pattern — because the ritual requires a Yarrow twin, and one must go into the well willingly. Beat: betrayal; love against duty made explicit.

chapters.title: Which One Came Home
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Evidence mounts that the survivor of the accident seven years ago may have been Marguerite wearing Sable's life — or that Sable is the drowned one given flesh again. His memories arrive in two voices. Beat: identity crisis peaks; the reader can no longer be certain who narrates.

chapters.title: The Bell Rings for You
chapters.summary: Village POV, choral. On the first snow, the bell rings thirteen times and every villager turns toward the Yarrow cottage. They come not with violence but with candles, singing the founders' hymn, asking him gently to come to the well. Beat: communal dread; tenderness as threat.

chapters.title: Running the White Roads
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Sable flees across the frozen fells, but every road bends back to Hollowmere; the village exists wherever he stops. In a bothy he finds his own missing-person poster, dated seven years ago. Beat: claustrophobic pursuit; escape revealed as impossible.

chapters.title: The First Founder's Daughter
chapters.summary: Sable's POV with the ghost of Elowen, first founder's daughter. Her spirit, kept warm in the church crypt, explains the ritual's true cost: not a life given, but a self divided — one twin above, one below, forever answering each other. Beat: the rules fully understood; a terrible symmetry revealed.

chapters.title: Solstice Eve
chapters.summary: Sable and Tam. The well stands three feet from brimming; the water has begun climbing the church walls inside. Tam offers to take Sable's place knowing it won't hold. Sable refuses — the ritual wants what it wants. Beat: loyalty tested; the choice narrowed to its cruelest form.

chapters.title: The Unfinished Verse
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Studying the founders' rite, Sable finds the sealing prayer ends mid-line — the founders never wrote the closing words because the closing words must be spoken by the one who goes down. The ritual cannot be completed from above. Beat: revelation that reframes everything; agency restored.

chapters.title: Descent
chapters.summary: Sable's POV, climax part one. On solstice night Sable walks into the well. Underwater he meets the other twin — Marguerite, or himself, faces interchangeable — and they speak the unfinished verse together, each supplying the other's half. Beat: love against duty resolved into shared sacrifice.

chapters.title: The Bell Falls Silent
chapters.summary: Village POV, choral. The bell rings once and cracks; the water recedes from the walls and sinks below the frost line. In the morning the register's final paired entry resolves into a single name, cleanly written. Beat: release; the village exhales for the first time in a century.

chapters.title: Spring Comes Late to Hollowmere
chapters.summary: Tam's POV. Weeks later, Tam tends a grave that holds, at last, a body — and plants snowdrops over it. The cottage upstairs is quiet now, but sometimes the pipes sing one note, like a hummed lullaby. Beat: mourning with warmth; ambiguity softened but intact.

chapters.title: Marguerite and the Winter
chapters.summary: Final chapter, Sable's POV — or the voice that answers to Sable. He stays in Hollowmere as its keeper, neither fully the twin who left nor the one who drowned, teaching the next generation the verse. Each solstice he visits the well and speaks his half of the line into the dark, and something kind answers. Beat: belonging achieved at the price of selfhood; bittersweet close.
